title: 2026 #30DayChartChallenge Retrospective
text:
For the past few years, I’ve sat on the sidelines while others created some really great visuals for the #30DayChartChallenge. This year, I decided to participate.
You can find my contributions to the challenge on my Posit Connect Cloud.
My goal was to hit all 30 days. Maybe going from 0 to 30 days was not a great plan because I missed that target. I only got 16, but still had lots of fun and learned a lot.
This post will reflect on that challenge, some of the charts I made, and some realizations I had along the way.

title: 2026 #30DayChartChallenge Retrospective
text:
Comparisons - Day 5: Experimental
My all-time favorite is from Comparisons - Day 5: Experimental.

I’ve been thinking about this type of visualization for years. I’ve always thought it would be interesting to have a Venn diagram where the size is proportional to the frequency of each group and the overlap proportional to the number of common values. Turns out, that already exists; it is just not commonly used. It is called a Euler diagram. This challenge gave me the opportunity to test it out, but I didn’t just want to do something novel, not just a single Euler diagram. I settled on a matrix plot. With this structure, I needed groups that have some qualitative trait that overlaps. I was initially thinking about species overlap in different ecosystems, but that data was difficult to find. I decided on diet overlap between predators in Florida waters. Even that was difficult to find in a standardized format. I’ll admit, the data is still not great, but it is the viz I wanted to focus on for this challenge. Overall, I think it turned out really well. As noted, this is an uncommon viz and I think it is pretty underutilized. I’m curious to see how this could be used in the future for other qualitative data.

title: 2026 #30DayChartChallenge Retrospective
text:
Distributions - Day 7: Multiscale
Next favorite is Distributions - Day 7: Multiscale.




You can also view this full-page in its own tab.
I like this one for two reasons. First, I got to explore a new tool. For this I used Observable JS within Quarto. This allowed me to apply the “Multiscale” theme from the prompt. The main view is the whole US, and you can click on a state to zoom into the specific state value. The second reason is because the data is something I am interested in. I’ve noticed in recent years there have been a lot of political moves and decisions that are centered around agriculture. Particularly, actions that destabilize or reduce agriculture. In my area, we are seeing lots of agricultural land being sold off for housing or commercial development. That is land that we will never get back. I wanted to see how prevalent this was in other areas. I definitely see myself looking into this data more, and I’m very interested in seeing when the next data cut comes.

title: 2026 #30DayChartChallenge Retrospective
text:
Relationships - Day 13: Ecosystems
My last favorite is Relationships - Day 13: Ecosystems.

This one was very fun to make because the data did not exist. Stardew Valley has a lot of its game stats in the Wiki, but not this data. Therefore, we had to collect the data. This involved several rounds of doing full runs through the mines. My partner played the game, and I recorded the data. This was also the plot where I learned something new and was almost immediately able to integrate it into my work. This plot required that I arrange distinct plots and images in a custom arrangement, moving and scaling as needed. This used functionality in the {patchwork} package that I have not encountered before, particularly wrap_elements(). This really helped in getting things arranged properly.

title: Biography
text:
By now, you’re probably thinking “Jack of all trades, master of none.” However, by working across many subjects, I quickly learned that data is data and the code used to work with the data is usually very similar.
This realization hit during my dissertation. My own research was in functional morphology, which is the intersection of morphology, ecology, and behavior. Lots of data in various forms. I was also assisting other graduate students in other labs, from fisheries and plant biology to climatology, with their modeling and code. Turns out, it was never a specific subject that was exciting, but the process of coding and analysis.
These days, I work with pharmaceutical data as a data programmer. Besides working with the data, I get to work on process automation, documentation tooling, and the infrastructure that makes research reproducible. Outside of work hours, I have a habit of chasing down cool biology, ecology, and conservation data to build something around. I find this rewarding because this data is often difficult to find, under-represented, and under-explored. I believe building tools and analyses around this data can bring meaningful change in these areas.
Below is a short résumé version of the story, which I’m always looking to expand.

Ensuring transfer and secure storage of client data.

Developing comprehensive documentation for analysis-ready datasets and model input files, ensuring accuracy and standardization of documentation, along with compliance with regulatory guidelines.

Special assignments:

Developed an internal R package for auto-creation of Quarto documents to display tables, figures, and listings.
Developed a resourcing Shiny app to align planned timeline with available workloads.
Developed a process to map files and programs to client directory systems, facilitating seamless integration and compliance with client standards while maintaining our standard directory structure.
Serve on committees to promote best R practices, improve secure file transfer to and from clients, update the standard directory structure, and ensure define compliance with regulatory bodies.

Inherited and overhauled a large R Shiny application built to present diverse environmental monitoring data to a Pacific Northwest state conservation commission, informing agricultural land management decisions. Refactored to modularize, improve load time, and add new data exploration features.

Processed and compiled data from dozens of sources including raw text parsing and external web interfaces for integration into the application.
Designed and implemented interactive visualizations across multiple data domains using Highcharter and Leaflet, including watershed water quality metrics (e.g., stage height, temperature, dissolved oxygen, phosphorus, TSS, turbidity, bacteria, and ammonia), NRCS conservation practice tracking, and USDA land use change.
Developed automated PDF reporting using Quarto and Typst, generating narratives and visual summaries of land use breakdowns by primary and subcategory classifications.

Graduate Researcher in Quantitative Biology



Melbourne, FL

Authored a 200+ page dissertation synthesizing large-scale morphological, taxonomic, environmental, and experimental analyses focused on cranial spine function across ray-finned fishes.

Collected, cleaned, and integrated over one billion data points in R from heterogeneous sources including global species occurrence databases, high-resolution environmental raster layers, and personally collected morphological measurements.
Extracted and engineered 100+ quantitative and qualitative morphological features describing cranial spine and body characteristics across 2,000+ ray-finned fish species. Applied hierarchical clustering to identify distinct spine morphology revealing taxonomic and cross-taxa expression patterns at the order, family, and genus level.
Built and compared an ensemble of predictive models including logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, and gradient boosting, to identify environmental variables most strongly associated with cranial spine expression.

title: Tidy Tuesday - 2020 - Week 33
text:
This is an old Tidy Tuesday post that I am moving to this new website.

Preparation


Code
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tvthemes)
library(extrafont)
# extrafont::fonts()
loadfonts(device = "win")
import_avatar()
# library(devtools)
# devtools::install_github("averyrobbins1/appa")
library(appa)

avatar <- appa::appa

scene_description2 <- avatar %>%
  select(id, scene_description) %>%
  unnest_longer(scene_description) %>%
  filter(!is.na(scene_description))

scene_description <- avatar %>%
  filter(character == "Scene Description") %>%
  select(-scene_description)

avatar <- avatar %>%
  filter(character != "Scene Description") %>%
  select(-scene_description)

# split where paired (ex. Aang and Zuko)
tosplit <- avatar %>%
  filter(str_detect(character, " and ")) %>%
  separate_rows(character, sep = " and ")

# remove rows with " and " then add in split rows and order
avatar <- avatar %>%
  filter(!str_detect(character, " and ")) %>%
  add_row(tosplit) %>%
  arrange(id)


# remove punctuation and count the number of words
avatar <- avatar %>%
  mutate(
    new_text = str_replace_all(character_words, "[[:punct:]]+", " "),
    numwords = str_count(new_text, "\\S+")
  )



# get the top characters based on number of words spoken (could'a told ya these)
topchars <- avatar %>%
  group_by(character) %>%
  summarise(words = sum(numwords)) %>%
  arrange(desc(words)) %>%
  top_n(n = 7) %>%
  ungroup()

# count number of words
words <- avatar %>%
  filter(character %in% topchars$character) %>%
  group_by(book_num, chapter_num, character) %>%
  summarise(words = sum(numwords)) %>%
  arrange(book_num, chapter_num, desc(words)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(chap_num_pad = str_pad(chapter_num, 2, pad = "0")) %>%
  select(-chapter_num) %>%
  unite("episode", c(book_num, chap_num_pad), sep = ".") %>%
  complete(episode, character) %>%
  replace_na(list(words = 0)) %>%
  group_by(character) %>%
  mutate(cumsum_words = cumsum(words)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(book = rep(rep(levels(
    factor(avatar$book)
  ), times = c(20, 20, 21)), each = 7),
  title = rep(levels(factor(avatar$chapter)), each = 7))




Plotting

title: Letters to Senators
text:
I’ve noticed a recurring pattern in several bits of proposed and passed legislation around tech that I’m concerned about. Not to get too much into the specific topic or my concerns other than saying that it deals with mandating that tech perform the operation of law enforcement; having the user of the tech prove each time they need to use the tech that they are not going to be operating in an illicit or illegal manner.
I feel strongly enough about this subject that I have the desire to write not just to my senators, but all 100 US senators.
Quarto was the first thought that came into my mind when thinking about how I was going to write 100 letters that need customized addresses, salutations, and text depending on the party affiliation of the specific senator.
I’ll go into details below on how I plan to write these letters following these steps.

Get data - pull name, party, and office address from the Senate’s contact page.
Get template - grab the letter Quarto/Typst template.
Modify Qmd - add parameterization to the template with conditional sections to customize per senator and party.

Construct letters - render all 100 PDFs.

Merge Letters - Merge into a single PDF for simplified printing.


1. Get data
senate.gov has an XML file with the information on all senators including names, office addresses, party, and more.
It is fairly simple to extract this information into a dataset.

library(xml2)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)

url <- "https://www.senate.gov/general/contact_information/senators_cfm.xml"
doc <- read_xml(url)
members <- xml_find_all(doc, "//member")

senators <- map_dfr(members, function(m) {
  tibble(
    first_name  = xml_text(xml_find_first(m, "./first_name")),
    last_name   = xml_text(xml_find_first(m, "./last_name")),
    party       = xml_text(xml_find_first(m, "./party")),
    state       = xml_text(xml_find_first(m, "./state")),
    office_address = trimws(gsub("\\s+", " ",
                                 xml_text(xml_find_first(m, "./address")))),
    split_address = str_replace(office_address, "Building ", "Building\n")
  )
})


write.csv(senators, "senators.csv", row.names = FALSE)

A few notes:

I’ve added a line break in the office_address to create the split_address so it can be more easily split into the usual two line address in letters.

I’ve exported as a CSV but you can easily pass this directly into step 4.



2. Get template
You could make your own Typst template, but there is already a great template built specifically for letter formatting with Quarto.
In your terminal, run the following: quarto use template quarto-ext/typst-templates/letter
It should ask a few questions including confirming whether you trust the source and if you want to construct this in a subdirectory. Since this is a small project, I’ve kept everything at the main R Project level. Two important things are made with this.
The first is the _extensions subfolder. This will hold several things, but mainly the Typst partials typst-template.typ and typst-show.typ.
The second is the qmd file. This will have the YAML heading which most importantly sets the format to use the letter-typst format, but also shows what inputs the template accepts. A few things to point out here. Most inputs are quoted, but the recipient is not and uses “\” to indicate line breaks. We don’t actually need any of this besides the format because we will be using quarto_render() and passing the other values in. You can remove everything from this qmd except the format, leaving just:
---
format:
  letter-typst: default
---


3. Modify Qmd
Now comes the fun part.
Let’s first add the parameterization aspect into the YAML header. Because the inputs like the senator’s name and address will be handled in the YAML header, the only real parameter I need here is the party. This will control certain text that varies depending on the party. So we are left with:
---
format:
  letter-typst: default
params: {party: null}
---
Now we can build the body.
There are several ways to add conditional text into the letter.
First, using conditionals within a chunk.
I would do this with medium bits of text that need to vary based on the party.
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

if(params$party == "D"){
  cat("Message for a democrat senator.")
} else if (params$party == "R"){
  cat("Message for a republican senator.")
} else {
  cat("Message for an independent senator.")
}
Second, you can use in-line conditionals. I’d use this for short differences like single sentences.
`r if (params$party == "D") "in-line message for a democrat senator" else
    if (params$party == "R") "in-line message for a republican senator" else
    "in-line message for an independent senator"`
Finally, you can make a chunk specifically for a specific condition. I would use this for paragraphs meant for a specific party. Use the eval option with !expr to tell Quarto to evaluate the following condition.
#| eval: !expr params$party == "I"
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

cat("Message for an independent senator.")
If you put this all together, you can get this qmd file.






Warning



The file downloads as _letter.qmd. If you’re dropping it into your own Quarto project, rename it to remove the leading underscore first.




4. Construct letters
With the qmd prepared, we can set up the parameterization.
First, let’s get the libraries for this next step and read in the CSV containing the senators’ information.

library(quarto)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(pdftools)

senators <- read.csv("senators.csv")

Next, we will iterate over each row.
This works in several steps.

Construct the text that goes into the recipient field.
Open the quarto_render() call.
Provide the qmd as the input.
Define the outputs. I struggle with getting this to output in a different directory, so this just outputs each to the current directory.
Pass in metadata. These are the inputs that were originally in the YAML header.
Pass in the execute_params, which in this case is just the party.

All of this combined gives the following.

pwalk(senators, function(first_name, last_name, party, split_address, ...) {
  
  recipient_text <- paste0(
    "Senator ", first_name, " ", last_name, " \\\n",
    "United States Senate \\\n",
    gsub("\n", " \\\n", split_address, fixed = TRUE)
  )
  
  quarto_render(
    input          = "letter.qmd",
    output_file    = paste0("letter_", last_name, ".pdf"),
    metadata = list(
      subject   = "Topic of Choice",
      name      = "Your Name",
      sender    = "Your Name, Your Address",
      recipient = recipient_text,
      sent      = paste0("Your City, ", format(Sys.Date(), "%B %d, %Y"))
    ),
    execute_params = list(
      party          = party
    )
  )
})

Run this to create all 100 letters.


5. Merge letters
Because I don’t want to have to deal with trying to organize 100 print jobs, I’d like to merge all of these together.
This only takes two lines.

pdf_files <- list.files(".", pattern = "letter_.*\\.pdf$", full.names = TRUE)

pdf_combine(pdf_files, output = "all_letters.pdf")

Now I have a single PDF containing all 100 letters, which I can print in a single print job.


Conclusion
Over the next week or so, I’ll customize the text for my specific topic and mail this out.
If you’ve got something to say to 100 people at once, parameterized Quarto make it a lot less painful.

title: IDE Settings - RStudio
text:
Rainbow Parentheses
Rainbow parentheses help keep track of your parentheses and brackets by coloring them in sets.
Turn them on by:
1 - Go to Tools
2 - Global Options…
3 - Code
4 - Display
5 - Check “Use rainbow parentheses”
Your parentheses and brackets will now look like: 


Pane Layout
Changing the pane layout can simplify your workflow.
The script and console both want to be tall, but they are stacked by default.
Putting them side-by-side can help line up your code and output.
To change the layout, click the Workspace Pane button then click “Console on the Right”
